title: Piano Tuners in a City
problem: Estimate how many full-time piano tuners a city of 2,000,000 people can support. State a transparent set of assumptions and identify which assumption matters most.

hints.text: Estimate households, piano ownership, tunings per piano per year, and jobs completed by one tuner per year.
One defensible model uses 2.5 people per household, 5% piano ownership, one tuning yearly, and 1,000 jobs per tuner-year.

solution.setup: Use demand divided by capacity, with explicit assumptions that can be challenged.
solution.reasoning: At 2.5 people per household there are about 800,000 households. If 5% own a piano, that is 40,000 pianos. At one tuning per year, demand is 40,000 jobs. A tuner completing four jobs per day for 250 days handles about 1,000 jobs annually, implying about 40 tuners. Piano ownership and tuning frequency are the most sensitive assumptions.
solution.finalAnswer: A reasonable central estimate is about 40 full-time tuners, plausibly within a broad range such as 15–100.
solution.sanityCheck: Forty tuners each serving 1,000 appointments accounts for the modeled 40,000 annual tunings.

keyInsight: A good Fermi estimate is a transparent model with units, not an unsupported guess.
recognitionCues: A population-scale question with no supplied data calls for decomposing demand and capacity.
commonMistakes: Presenting a precise number without stating assumptions or uncertainty.
followUps: How would the estimate change for a university town or a city with smaller households?

source.notes: Original Fermi-estimation exercise in a classic problem family.
